raw_text:
Peripartum cardiomyopathy (PPCM) is an idiopathic systolic heart failure syndrome presenting near the end of pregnancy or in the months after delivery, in the absence of another identifiable cause. Early descriptions emphasized a distinct natural history, and modern definitions generally require left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) <45%, with or without ventricular dilatation [1-3]. The condition occupies a unique interface between cardiology, obstetrics, genetics, vascular biology and critical care: it may resolve completely, yet it remains an important cause of maternal morbidity and mortality worldwide [4-7].

Reported incidence varies widely by geography and ascertainment, from uncommon in many European cohorts to substantially more frequent in parts of Africa and among women of African ancestry in North America [8-11]. Consistent risk factors include advanced maternal age, multiparity, multifetal gestation, hypertensive disorders of pregnancy, pre-eclampsia, and African ancestry; socioeconomic and access-to-care factors probably modify observed outcomes [8-11]. Population-based studies suggest increasing recognition over time, although true incidence may also be rising with older maternal age, assisted reproduction and cardiometabolic comorbidity [8,10].

Pathophysiology is multifactorial. A central experimental model links late gestational oxidative stress to cleavage of prolactin into a 16-kDa antiangiogenic and proapoptotic fragment; this provides a rationale for prolactin blockade with bromocriptine in selected patients [12,13,23,24]. A complementary vascular hypothesis implicates antiangiogenic imbalance, particularly excess soluble fms-like tyrosine kinase-1, explaining the association with pre-eclampsia and twin pregnancy [14,17]. Inflammation, endothelial dysfunction, micronutrient deficiency and maladaptive immune responses may contribute, but are unlikely to explain all cases [12,18,19]. Genetic susceptibility is increasingly recognized: truncating variants, especially in TTN, overlap with dilated cardiomyopathy, supporting the concept that pregnancy can unmask latent myocardial vulnerability [15,16].

Clinically, PPCM often presents with dyspnoea, orthopnoea, cough, edema, fatigue, palpitations or chest discomfort. Because normal pregnancy produces dyspnoea and edema, diagnosis is frequently delayed. Red flags include resting tachycardia, hypoxaemia, pulmonary rales, elevated jugular venous pressure, new murmur, cardiomegaly, pulmonary edema, syncope or thromboembolism. Evaluation should include electrocardiography, natriuretic peptide testing, echocardiography and assessment for alternative diagnoses such as pulmonary embolism, valvular disease, congenital heart disease, myocarditis, ischemia, thyroid disease and severe pre-eclampsia. Echocardiography establishes LVEF, ventricular size, right ventricular function, pulmonary pressures, valvular regurgitation and intracardiac thrombus. Cardiac magnetic resonance may be useful postpartum when myocarditis, scar or infiltrative disease is suspected, but gadolinium is usually avoided during pregnancy unless essential.

Management depends on gestational timing, severity and fetal status. During pregnancy, therapy must balance maternal stabilization with fetal safety. Diuretics relieve congestion; beta-blockers, hydralazine and nitrates are commonly used; digoxin may be considered. Angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers, angiotensin receptor–neprilysin inhibitors, mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists and sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors are generally avoided before delivery. Anticoagulation is considered for severe LV dysfunction, atrial fibrillation, intracardiac thrombus, bromocriptine use or other thrombotic risk, because pregnancy and early puerperium are hypercoagulable [7,30]. Delivery is indicated for obstetric reasons or refractory maternal instability; otherwise, vaginal delivery with careful haemodynamic management is often preferred. Mechanical circulatory support and transplantation are reserved for shock or refractory advanced heart failure.

After delivery, guideline-directed medical therapy for heart failure with reduced ejection fraction should be instituted and titrated as tolerated, taking breastfeeding compatibility into account [7,28-30]. Bromocriptine has shown signals of benefit in small and moderate-sized studies, particularly when combined with standard heart failure therapy, but it requires thromboprophylaxis and careful individualized discussion because it suppresses lactation [23,24]. Implantable cardioverter-defibrillator placement is usually deferred for several months because LV recovery is common; wearable defibrillators may be considered in high-risk patients.

Prognosis is heterogeneous. Contemporary North American and European cohorts show substantial recovery, commonly within 6–12 months, but persistent LV dysfunction, relapse, arrhythmia, thromboembolism and death still occur [18-22,27]. Poor prognostic markers include very low presenting LVEF, marked LV dilatation, right ventricular dysfunction, delayed diagnosis, elevated natriuretic peptides or troponin, and some genetic variants [16,18,21,22]. Subsequent pregnancy requires specialist counselling. Women with persistent LV dysfunction face high risk of deterioration and adverse maternal outcomes; even after apparent recovery, relapse can occur, so preconception assessment and close multidisciplinary surveillance are essential [25]. Overall, PPCM should be approached as a potentially reversible but high-risk cardiomyopathy requiring early recognition, coordinated cardio-obstetric care, long-term follow-up and individualized reproductive counselling.
